ann_23.text: This part of the model, which reads a3 and a5, barely changes the predictions.

ann_24.text: This part of the model acts on 120 of the 345 training cases, and 16 of them are actually 'yes'.
For the typical case it acts on, which has every attribute at its first value, it slightly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 2% to below 1%.
Through this part, moving a6 away from its first value slightly raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes', and giving a2 or a4 its first value slightly lowers it, all staying below 1%.
Moving a3 away from its first value or giving a1 the value 3 slightly raises it as well (on the training data only).
The effects of a2, a3 and a4 through this part are also slightly larger when a3 = 1 or a6 = 1.

ann_25.text: This part of the model acts on the 85 training cases with a5 = 3, and 28 of them are actually 'yes'.

For the typical case it acts on (a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 3, a6 = 1), it lowers the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 91% without the part to about 85% with it (on the training data only).

For that case, changing a4 from 2 to another value through this part slightly raises it, from about 85% to about 87%, and through it a5 = 3 slightly lowers the predicted probability compared with a5 = 1 (on the training data only).
In the model, the rise from a5 = 1 to a5 = 3 is slightly larger when a4 is other than 2 (to about 87%) than when a4 = 2 (to about 85%).

ann_26.text: Through this part, giving a4 its first value slightly raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes', and moving a3 away from its first value slightly lowers it, both staying below 1%.
Changing a2 from 3 to 1 also slightly raises it, and moving a1 or a6 away from its first value, giving a5 the value 2 or changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly lowers it (on the training data only).

ann_27.text: This part of the model reads only a5; through it, moving a5 away from its first value raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 91% (on the training data only).

ann_28.text: For the typical case, moving a5 away from its first value raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 91% for a5 = 4, about 85% for a5 = 3 and about 79% for a5 = 2 (on the training data only).
Changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly lowers it and changing a4 from 2 to 3 slightly raises it, both staying below 1%.
Changing a1 from 1 to 2 slightly lowers it too (on the training data only).

ann_23.original: An inert serial chain. Node 611 = ReLU(0.212*z(a3:1) - 1.458); z(a3:1) takes only two values (-1.03, +0.97), so its pre-activation is at most -1.25 and 611 is identically zero. Node 1057 = ReLU(0.143*z(a5:4) + 0.572*h611 - 2.649); with h611 = 0 its pre-activation is at most -2.40, so 1057 is identically zero and its -0.125 readout contributes nothing. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivity 0 for both entries; exhaustive enumeration of all 432 inputs gives h611 = h1057 = 0 everywhere. Structurally present, functionally absent.
ann_23.proposed: This part barely changes the predictions.

ann_24.original: A graded count gate over four of the six rule indicators. In indicator terms the pre-activation of 1158 is -13.56 + 8.28[a3=1] + 6.59[a2=1] + 5.58[a4=1] + 5.62[a6=1] - 1.68[a1=3] (a3 enters through its complement a3:2, weight -4.14). It fires iff at least three of {a2=1,a3=1,a4=1,a6=1} hold (activation >= 2.56) or a3=1 plus exactly one other with a1!=3 (activation only 0.30..1.31). a1=1 and a5=1 are not consulted. Readout -6.92, so the penalty to the output logit is graded: about -2.1 to -9.1 for the a3+one pairs, -17.7 to -86.6 for three or more. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivities (a3:2 1.44, a2:1 1.08, a6:1 0.98, a4:1 0.90, a1:3 0.27); exhaustive enumeration confirms the firing rule on 432/432 inputs. Role: the upper edge of the response peak (suppresses inputs with too many indicators), but the weak pair-level activation is not always enough to cancel the ramp (e.g. a1=1,a3=1,a6=1 stays positive).
ann_24.proposed: This part acts on 120 training cases, 16 of them actually 'yes', and slightly lowers their predicted probability of 'yes'; through it, first values of a2 and a4 slightly lower it and a6 away from its first value slightly raises it.

ann_25.original: A small a5=3 detector. In indicator terms 708 = ReLU(-3.37 + 5.59[a5=3] + 0.69[a4=2] - 0.72[a5=1]): 2.22 when a5=3 (2.92 if also a4=2), zero otherwise. Readout -0.207 lowers the logit by 0.46/0.60 when a5=3. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivity dominated by a5:3 (0.59 vs 0.08 for a4:2 and a5:1); enumeration shows three values {0, 2.22, 2.92}; removing it flips the decision on only 9/432 inputs. A minor nuisance term.
ann_25.proposed: A small a5 = 3 term that lowers the predicted probability of 'yes' for the cases with a5 = 3 (on the training data only).

ann_26.original: An additive ramp over the first-value indicators of a1,a2,a3,a4,a6. Node 3057 = ReLU(1.51*z(a2:3)+1.73) is always active (0.641 or 3.826), so it is a linear term in a2:3. Per attribute, relative to all attributes at their second value (ramp = -10.37): a1=1 +1.25; a2=1 +5.24 (a2=3 +0.73); a3=1 +3.70; a4=1 +2.28; a6=1 +4.05; a5=2 -1.05 relative to a5=1/3/4. The ramp therefore rises roughly linearly with the number of strong indicators (a2,a3,a4,a6), with a1=1 weighted only weakly; with the output bias, the a5 veto offset and no gate it crosses zero once about two strong indicators are present (or one strong indicator plus a1=1 in some combinations): the lower edge of the response peak. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivities match the edge weights; exhaustive enumeration confirms exact additivity.
ann_26.proposed: An additive score through which a4 = 1 slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' and a3 away from its first value slightly lowers it, with further small effects of a1, a2, a5 and a6 on the training data only.

ann_27.original: A veto on a5=1. The direct edge a5:1 -> output has weight -6.82 on the z-score: +3.96 when a5!=1, -11.74 when a5=1, a jump of -15.70. The remaining terms cannot overcome it (max ramp gain from indicators is +16.5 from a baseline of -20.7 with a5=1, and the gate subtracts once several indicators are present), so the network never predicts class 1 when a5=1. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivity 6.82; enumeration: 0 of 108 a5=1 inputs positive.
ann_27.proposed: A switch on a5: any value other than 1 raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' to about 91% (on the training data only).

ann_28.original: The output composes the five children additively under the final sigmoid: logit = 0.371 + Ramp + Veto - 6.921*Gate - 0.207*A5_3 - 0.125*Inert (Inert identically zero). Inputs a1:2 and a4:3 have no enabled connections and are zero-effect entries. With a5 in {3,4} the baseline logit is about -4.99; the ramp adds a1=1 +1.25, a2=1 +5.24, a3=1 +3.70, a4=1 +2.28, a6=1 +4.05, so it turns positive once about two strong indicators (a2,a3,a4,a6) are present (lower edge of a response peak). The count gate pulls the logit back down when three of {a2,a3,a4,a6} are first-valued (upper edge), weakly also for a3 plus one other. The a5=1 veto makes the output negative whenever a5=1; a5=3 subtracts a further 0.46-0.60. Net: an approximate 'about two of {a2,a3,a4,a6} (a1 weak), and a5 must not be 1' peak detector. Evidence: closed form composition; train sensitivity of the output (gate 0.53, ramp and veto 0.076 each, 708 0.016, 1057 0.010, unconnected 0); enumeration: 111/432 positive; by total indicator count k: k=0 0%, k=1 4%, k=2 54%, k=3 27%, k>=4 0%. Against the MONK-2 target: 65 false negatives all at k=2 (28 with a5=1 vetoed; 16 a3+one-other pairs suppressed by the gate; 21 where the ramp is too weak: 20 pairs a1=1 with a3, a4 or a6, plus one a3+a4 pair with a1=3), 34 false positives (30 at k=3, mostly a1=1 plus two others where the gate is weak or silent; 4 at k=1 with a2=1 alone). Changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly lowers it and changing a4 from 2 to 3 slightly raises it, both staying below 1%.
Changing a1 from 1 to 2 slightly lowers it too (on the training data only).

One part of the model acts on 120 of the 345 training cases, 16 of which are actually 'yes', and for the typical case it acts on, which has every attribute at its first value, it slightly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 2% to below 1%.
One small part of the model, which reads a3 and a5, barely changes the predictions.

parts.name: peak_with_a5_veto
parts.original_hypothesis: The output composes the five children additively under the final sigmoid: logit = 0.371 + Ramp + Veto - 6.921*Gate - 0.207*A5_3 - 0.125*Inert (Inert identically zero). Inputs a1:2 and a4:3 have no enabled connections and are zero-effect entries. With a5 in {3,4} the baseline logit is about -4.99; the ramp adds a1=1 +1.25, a2=1 +5.24, a3=1 +3.70, a4=1 +2.28, a6=1 +4.05, so it turns positive once about two strong indicators (a2,a3,a4,a6) are present (lower edge of a response peak). The count gate pulls the logit back down when three of {a2,a3,a4,a6} are first-valued (upper edge), weakly also for a3 plus one other. The a5=1 veto makes the output negative whenever a5=1; a5=3 subtracts a further 0.46-0.60. Net: an approximate 'about two of {a2,a3,a4,a6} (a1 weak), and a5 must not be 1' peak detector. Evidence: closed form composition; train sensitivity of the output (gate 0.53, ramp and veto 0.076 each, 708 0.016, 1057 0.010, unconnected 0); enumeration: 111/432 positive; by total indicator count k: k=0 0%, k=1 4%, k=2 54%, k=3 27%, k>=4 0%. Against the MONK-2 target: 65 false negatives all at k=2 (28 with a5=1 vetoed; 16 a3+one-other pairs suppressed by the gate; 21 where the ramp is too weak: 20 pairs a1=1 with a3, a4 or a6, plus one a3+a4 pair with a1=3), 34 false positives (30 at k=3, mostly a1=1 plus two others where the gate is weak or silent; 4 at k=1 with a2=1 alone). Train accuracy 0.786, AUC 0.794; function preservation error 3.3e-16.

parts.name: count_gate_a2_a3_a4_a6
parts.original_hypothesis: A graded count gate over four of the six rule indicators. In indicator terms the pre-activation of 1158 is -13.56 + 8.28[a3=1] + 6.59[a2=1] + 5.58[a4=1] + 5.62[a6=1] - 1.68[a1=3] (a3 enters through its complement a3:2, weight -4.14). It fires iff at least three of {a2=1,a3=1,a4=1,a6=1} hold (activation >= 2.56) or a3=1 plus exactly one other with a1!=3 (activation only 0.30..1.31). a1=1 and a5=1 are not consulted. Readout -6.92, so the penalty to the output logit is graded: about -2.1 to -9.1 for the a3+one pairs, -17.7 to -86.6 for three or more. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivities (a3:2 1.44, a2:1 1.08, a6:1 0.98, a4:1 0.90, a1:3 0.27); exhaustive enumeration confirms the firing rule on 432/432 inputs. Role: the upper edge of the response peak (suppresses inputs with too many indicators), but the weak pair-level activation is not always enough to cancel the ramp (e.g. a1=1,a3=1,a6=1 stays positive).

parts.name: a5_1_veto
parts.original_hypothesis: A veto on a5=1. The direct edge a5:1 -> output has weight -6.82 on the z-score: +3.96 when a5!=1, -11.74 when a5=1, a jump of -15.70. The remaining terms cannot overcome it (max ramp gain from indicators is +16.5 from a baseline of -20.7 with a5=1, and the gate subtracts once several indicators are present), so the network never predicts class 1 when a5=1. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivity 6.82; enumeration: 0 of 108 a5=1 inputs positive.

parts.name: linear_indicator_ramp
parts.original_hypothesis: An additive ramp over the first-value indicators of a1,a2,a3,a4,a6. Node 3057 = ReLU(1.51*z(a2:3)+1.73) is always active (0.641 or 3.826), so it is a linear term in a2:3. Per attribute, relative to all attributes at their second value (ramp = -10.37): a1=1 +1.25; a2=1 +5.24 (a2=3 +0.73); a3=1 +3.70; a4=1 +2.28; a6=1 +4.05; a5=2 -1.05 relative to a5=1/3/4. The ramp therefore rises roughly linearly with the number of strong indicators (a2,a3,a4,a6), with a1=1 weighted only weakly; with the output bias, the a5 veto offset and no gate it crosses zero once about two strong indicators are present (or one strong indicator plus a1=1 in some combinations): the lower edge of the response peak. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivities match the edge weights; exhaustive enumeration confirms exact additivity.

parts.name: a5_3_minor_penalty
parts.original_hypothesis: A small a5=3 detector. In indicator terms 708 = ReLU(-3.37 + 5.59[a5=3] + 0.69[a4=2] - 0.72[a5=1]): 2.22 when a5=3 (2.92 if also a4=2), zero otherwise. Readout -0.207 lowers the logit by 0.46/0.60 when a5=3. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivity dominated by a5:3 (0.59 vs 0.08 for a4:2 and a5:1); enumeration shows three values {0, 2.22, 2.92}; removing it flips the decision on only 9/432 inputs. A minor nuisance term.

parts.name: inert_chain_a3_a5
parts.original_hypothesis: An inert serial chain. Node 611 = ReLU(0.212*z(a3:1) - 1.458); z(a3:1) takes only two values (-1.03, +0.97), so its pre-activation is at most -1.25 and 611 is identically zero. Node 1057 = ReLU(0.143*z(a5:4) + 0.572*h611 - 2.649); with h611 = 0 its pre-activation is at most -2.40, so 1057 is identically zero and its -0.125 readout contributes nothing. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivity 0 for both entries; exhaustive enumeration of all 432 inputs gives h611 = h1057 = 0 everywhere. Structurally present, functionally absent.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
